source.name: ASTRA chemistry practice set
source.license: Original syllabus-based practice questions (exam-frequent themes; not verbatim past papers)

questions.stem: An ionic bond is formed primarily by
options: transfer of electrons from a metal atom to a non-metal atom
equal sharing of an electron pair between identical atoms
overlap of only d orbitals on neighbouring metals
questions.explanation: The metal loses valence electrons and the non-metal gains them, giving ions that attract electrostatically.

questions.stem: A covalent bond between two atoms arises when
options: electrons are transferred completely from one atom to the other
a shared pair of electrons occupies the internuclear region
the two nuclei fuse into one
questions.explanation: Covalent bonding is mutual sharing of electron pairs that sit between the bonded nuclei.

questions.stem: In a coordinate (dative) covalent bond, the shared electron pair
options: is contributed equally, one electron from each atom
is donated entirely by one of the two atoms
is lost from both atoms into the crystal lattice
questions.explanation: Both electrons of a coordinate bond come from the donor atom; after formation the link looks like an ordinary covalent bond.

questions.stem: Formation of NH4+ from ammonia and H+ involves
options: a purely ionic NaCl-type lattice with no sharing
a coordinate bond in which nitrogen donates a lone pair to H+
a metallic bond between nitrogen atoms
replacement of all N-H covalent links by hydrogen bonds
questions.explanation: The lone pair on nitrogen is donated to the bare proton, giving a coordinate N→H link in ammonium.

questions.stem: The Lewis octet rule states that many main-group atoms tend to
options: attain eight electrons in the valence shell
keep an odd number of valence electrons
questions.explanation: Atoms of the second period especially share or transfer electrons so that eight valence electrons surround each atom.

questions.stem: Which of these species has an incomplete octet on the central atom?
questions.explanation: Boron in BF3 is surrounded by only six valence electrons after three B-F bonds.

questions.stem: SF6 is a textbook example of a molecule with
questions.explanation: Sulphur uses vacant 3d orbitals and is surrounded by twelve electrons from six S-F bonds.

questions.stem: Nitric oxide (NO) is called an odd-electron molecule because
options: nitrogen expands its octet to ten electrons
the molecule contains one unpaired electron
both atoms already have complete octets with no leftover electron
questions.explanation: NO has eleven valence electrons, so one electron remains unpaired in a Lewis picture.

questions.stem: Crystalline sodium chloride is held together mainly by
options: covalent sharing of a Na-Cl electron pair
electrostatic attraction between Na+ and Cl- ions
a metallic sea of electrons from chlorine
questions.explanation: After electron transfer, the ionic lattice is stabilised by Coulomb attraction of opposite charges.

questions.stem: The adduct H3N→BF3 is a classic illustration of
options: ionic lattice energy of a salt
a coordinate covalent bond from nitrogen to boron
questions.explanation: Ammonia donates its nitrogen lone pair into the empty orbital of boron trifluoride.

questions.stem: Ionic character is favoured when the metal has
options: high ionisation enthalpy and the non-metal has low electron-gain enthalpy
low ionisation enthalpy and the non-metal has high electron-gain enthalpy
electronegativity identical to that of the non-metal
a very large cation and a tiny anion as the only requirement
questions.explanation: Easy loss of electrons by the metal and easy gain by the non-metal promote ion formation.

questions.stem: The dimer Al2Cl6 contains, in addition to ordinary Al-Cl covalent bonds,
options: only ionic Al3+ and Cl- with no sharing
coordinate bonds from bridging chlorine atoms to aluminium
metallic Al-Al bonds like in aluminium metal
questions.explanation: Each aluminium is electron-deficient; a lone pair on a bridging chlorine is donated to the neighbouring Al.

questions.stem: Phosphorus pentachloride violates a strict octet because
options: phosphorus uses empty 3d orbitals and is surrounded by ten electrons
each chlorine atom expands its octet to ten electrons
the formula is ionic P5+ with five Cl- and no covalency
the molecule has one unpaired electron
questions.explanation: P in PCl5 has five bond pairs (ten electrons). Third-period elements can expand the octet using 3d orbitals.

questions.stem: Gaseous BeCl2 is described as electron-deficient because beryllium then has
options: only four valence electrons after forming two Be-Cl covalent bonds
a complete octet of eight electrons
an incomplete octet on chlorine rather than on beryllium
an unpaired electron and is therefore a radical
questions.explanation: Be starts with two valence electrons and shares them in two bonds, leaving only four electrons around Be.

questions.stem: Molten NaCl conducts electricity, whereas solid sucrose does not, mainly because
options: sucrose molecules carry a net charge in the crystal
NaCl supplies mobile ions while sucrose is a molecular covalent solid
sucrose is a metallic conductor when cold
questions.explanation: Ionic melts have free ions that carry current; molecular covalent sucrose has no mobile charged particles.

questions.stem: Among gaseous BeCl2, solid NaCl and diamond, the dominant bonding types are respectively
options: electron-deficient covalent, ionic, giant covalent network
questions.explanation: BeCl2(g) has two covalent bonds and an incomplete octet; NaCl is ionic; diamond is a covalent network of sp3 carbon.

questions.stem: Formal charge on an atom in a Lewis structure equals
options: valence electrons minus lone-pair electrons minus half the shared electrons
the oxidation number in every case
the molecular dipole moment in debye
questions.explanation: FC = V − N − B/2, where V is valence electrons, N is non-bonding electrons and B is bonding electrons.

questions.stem: In a common canonical form of ozone, the central oxygen atom carries a formal charge of
questions.explanation: Central O has six valence electrons, one lone pair and three bonds, so FC = 6 − 2 − 3 = +1.

questions.stem: Resonance in the carbonate ion means that
options: the carbon atom physically jumps among the three oxygens
the real ion is a hybrid of three equivalent Lewis forms
only one C=O double bond exists as a fixed localisation
the ion is paramagnetic with an unpaired electron
questions.explanation: The three C-O bonds are identical; the pi electron pair is delocalised over the whole ion.

questions.stem: All N-O linkages in the nitrate ion are equivalent because of
options: purely ionic attraction with no pi bonding
resonance delocalisation of the pi bond over the three oxygens
hybridisation of oxygen alone with no delocalisation
questions.explanation: Three canonical forms share the double bond equally, so every N-O bond is the same.

questions.stem: Canonical (resonating) structures of a hybrid
options: exist as rapidly interconverting real molecules that can be isolated
are imaginary contributing drawings, not separately existing species
must have different nuclear positions from one another
questions.explanation: Resonance forms are bookkeeping pictures; the molecule has one blended electronic structure.

questions.stem: The more acceptable Lewis structure is generally the one with
options: formal charges closest to zero, with any negative charge on the more electronegative atom
the greatest number of unpaired electrons
questions.explanation: Low formal charges and placing negative charge on F, O or N give a better description.

questions.stem: Benzene is more stable than a hypothetical localised cyclohexatriene mainly because of
options: ionic bonding between carbon and hydrogen
resonance energy from delocalised pi electrons
questions.explanation: Delocalisation of six pi electrons over the ring lowers the energy relative to three isolated double bonds.

questions.stem: A satisfactory Lewis picture of carbon monoxide places
options: a C≡O triple bond with formal charges −1 on carbon and +1 on oxygen
only a C-O single bond and no lone pairs
a complete octet on carbon with no lone pair on carbon
questions.explanation: :C≡O: gives carbon an octet. Formal charges are −1 (C) and +1 (O), which matches the small dipole with carbon at the negative end.

questions.stem: Resonance in ozone explains why
options: the two O-O distances are equal and lie between single- and double-bond lengths
one O-O link is a pure single bond and the other a pure triple bond
the molecule is linear like CO2
ozone is diamagnetic with a bond order of three
questions.explanation: Two equivalent forms average the bonds, so both O-O links are identical and of intermediate length.

questions.stem: The average N-O bond order in NO3- is
questions.explanation: Four bonding pairs are shared among three N-O links, so the bond order is 4/3.

questions.stem: The formal charge on nitrogen in the ammonium ion is
questions.explanation: FC = 5 − 0 − 8/2 = +1; nitrogen still has an octet but the ion carries the extra positive charge.

questions.stem: In carbonate ion the carbon-oxygen bond order is
questions.explanation: Four electron pairs are delocalised over three C-O bonds, giving bond order 4/3 ≈ 1.33.

questions.stem: For N2O the skeleton N-N-O is preferred over N-O-N because
options: it allows smaller formal charges on the atoms
oxygen must occupy the central position in every triatomic
N2O is an ionic lattice of N2+ and O-
resonance is impossible for an N-N-O arrangement
questions.explanation: N-N-O drawings give formal charges near zero; N-O-N forces large, less acceptable charges.

questions.stem: An ozone canonical form that puts like charges on adjacent oxygen atoms is
options: only a minor contributor, because adjacent like charges raise the energy
the only structure that actually exists
required by the octet rule and therefore dominant
questions.explanation: Structures with neighbouring +/+ or −/− charges are high in energy and contribute little to the hybrid.

questions.stem: Bond length between a given pair of atoms generally decreases as
options: atomic size increases with nothing else changed
temperature is lowered with no change in bonding
questions.explanation: More shared electron pairs pull the nuclei closer, so a triple bond is shorter than a double or single bond.

questions.stem: Bond enthalpy is defined as the energy needed to
options: form one mole of bonds from gaseous atoms with no other change
break one mole of a specified bond in gaseous molecules
ionise a molecule to a cation
questions.explanation: It is the enthalpy change for homolytic cleavage of that bond in the gas phase.

questions.stem: Compared with a carbon-carbon single bond, a carbon-carbon triple bond is
questions.explanation: Bond order 3 means greater electron density between the carbons, so the link is both shorter and stronger.

questions.stem: The H-C-H bond angle in methane is approximately
questions.explanation: Four equivalent C-H bonds around carbon give the tetrahedral angle of about 109.5°.

questions.stem: Among single, double and triple bonds between the same two atoms, the triple bond has the
options: same strength as the single bond
questions.explanation: Higher bond order raises the energy required to separate the atoms.

questions.stem: The covalent radius of an atom is taken as roughly
options: half the internuclear distance in a homonuclear single-bonded molecule
the van der Waals radius of the isolated atom
always equal to the metallic radius
the ionic radius of the corresponding cation
questions.explanation: For X2, r_cov ≈ (X-X single-bond length)/2.

questions.stem: Bond angle means the angle between
options: a nucleus and a lone pair with no bonded atom
two bond axes that originate from the same atom
the two ends of the molecular dipole vector
hybrid orbitals belonging to two different atoms
questions.explanation: It is the internuclear angle A-B-C at the central atom B.

questions.stem: The H-O-H angle in water is less than the tetrahedral angle mainly because
options: lone-pair–bond-pair repulsion compresses the bond angle
hydrogen is more electronegative than oxygen
questions.explanation: Two lone pairs on oxygen occupy more space than bond pairs, so the H-O-H angle falls to about 104.5°.

questions.stem: The F-F bond dissociation enthalpy is lower than that of Cl-Cl largely because
options: fluorine is less electronegative than chlorine
lone-pair repulsion is severe in the small F2 molecule
chlorine atoms have no lone pairs
questions.explanation: The short F-F distance forces non-bonding pairs to crowd, weakening the bond despite fluorine’s high electronegativity.

questions.stem: In the hydrogen halide series, H-F has the
options: longest bond and the lowest bond enthalpy
shortest bond and the highest bond enthalpy
purely ionic character with no covalent radius
questions.explanation: Fluorine is the smallest halogen, so H-F is the shortest and strongest of the H-X bonds.

questions.stem: Increasing s-character in a hybrid orbital of carbon
options: lengthens the bond and lowers its enthalpy
shortens the bond and raises bond enthalpy
converts every sigma bond into a pi bond
questions.explanation: An sp carbon (50% s) holds electrons closer than sp3 (25% s), so C-H and C-C bonds become shorter and stronger.

questions.stem: The observed H-N-H angle in ammonia is about 107° rather than 109.5° because
options: the lone pair occupies more space than a bond pair and compresses the angles
hydrogen bonding forces NH3 to become linear
questions.explanation: lp-bp repulsion > bp-bp repulsion, so the three N-H bonds are squeezed slightly below the tetrahedral value.

questions.stem: A polar covalent bond develops when the bonded atoms
options: differ in electronegativity so the shared pair is displaced
must belong to a linear molecule
questions.explanation: The more electronegative atom draws the shared pair closer and acquires a partial negative charge.

questions.stem: According to Fajan’s rules, a cation polarises an anion more strongly if the cation is
options: isoelectronic with neon and nothing else
questions.explanation: High charge density on a small, highly charged cation distorts the anion’s electron cloud.

questions.stem: Polarisability of an anion increases with
options: increasing ionisation enthalpy of the parent atom
decreasing atomic number at constant size
questions.explanation: A large, highly charged anion holds its outer electrons loosely, so they are easily distorted.

questions.stem: Among the alkali-metal chlorides, covalent character is greatest in
questions.explanation: Li+ is the smallest alkali cation and therefore the most polarising, so LiCl is the most covalent.

questions.stem: The unit commonly used for molecular dipole moment is the
questions.explanation: Dipole moment is quoted in debye (D); 1 D = 3.33564 × 10^−30 C m.

questions.stem: Water has a permanent dipole moment because the molecule is
options: linear, so the two O-H bond dipoles cancel
bent, so the two O-H bond dipoles do not cancel
built from oxygen and hydrogen of equal electronegativity
questions.explanation: The bent shape leaves a net dipole pointing toward oxygen.

questions.stem: Polarising power of a cation increases with its
questions.explanation: A high charge on a small cation gives a strong polarising field.

questions.stem: AgCl is more covalent than NaCl because Ag+
options: is larger than Na+ and therefore less polarising
has a pseudo noble-gas (18-electron) configuration that polarises Cl- strongly
questions.explanation: Cations with an 18-electron outer shell polarise anions more than noble-gas cations of similar size.

questions.stem: The dipole moment of a bond equals the product of
options: the magnitude of the separated charges and the internuclear distance
mass and velocity of the molecule
bond order and bond enthalpy only
questions.explanation: μ = q × d for a charge separation q over distance d.

questions.stem: Boron trifluoride has a net dipole of zero because
options: the B-F bonds are completely nonpolar
the molecule is trigonal planar and the three bond dipoles cancel
fluorine is electropositive relative to boron
questions.explanation: Three equal B-F dipoles at 120° in a plane sum to zero, even though each bond is polar.

questions.stem: Carbon dioxide is nonpolar while sulphur dioxide is polar because
options: CO2 is linear so bond dipoles cancel, whereas SO2 is bent
questions.explanation: Opposite C=O dipoles cancel in linear CO2; the bent SO2 molecule has a net dipole toward sulphur’s lone pair.

questions.stem: Percentage ionic character from measured dipole moment is given by
options: μ_ionic / μ_observed with no factor of 100
a constant 50% for every heteronuclear bond
questions.explanation: Comparing the observed μ with q × d for full charge transfer estimates the ionic contribution.

questions.stem: NH3 has a dipole moment whereas BF3 does not, mainly because
options: NH3 is pyramidal with a lone pair, while BF3 is trigonal planar
boron is more electronegative than nitrogen
questions.explanation: The lone pair on nitrogen and the unsymmetrical shape give NH3 a net dipole; BF3’s planar bond dipoles cancel.

questions.stem: NF3 has a smaller dipole moment than NH3 because
options: fluorine is less electronegative than hydrogen
N-F bond dipoles oppose the lone-pair moment, whereas N-H dipoles reinforce it
questions.explanation: In NF3 the bond dipoles point toward fluorine, partly cancelling the lone-pair contribution; in NH3 they add to it.

questions.stem: BeCl2 is more covalent than BaCl2 because
options: Be2+ is much smaller and more polarising than Ba2+
chlorine is a different element in the two chlorides
BeCl2 is purely ionic with an exceptionally high lattice energy
questions.explanation: Fajan: the tiny, highly polarising Be2+ distorts Cl- and the chloride is largely covalent.

questions.stem: CCl4 has zero net dipole whereas CHCl3 does not, because
options: C-Cl bonds in CCl4 are nonpolar
tetrahedral CCl4 bond dipoles cancel, while CHCl3 is unsymmetrical
carbon cannot form polar bonds at all
questions.explanation: Four identical C-Cl dipoles arranged tetrahedrally sum to zero; replacing one Cl by H destroys that cancellation.

questions.stem: VSEPR theory predicts molecular geometry from
options: nuclear spin of the central atom
repulsion among valence electron pairs around the central atom
questions.explanation: Electron pairs stay as far apart as possible; the resulting arrangement is the observed shape.

questions.stem: The water molecule is best described as
questions.explanation: Two bond pairs and two lone pairs on oxygen give a tetrahedral electron geometry and a bent molecular shape.

questions.stem: Gaseous beryllium chloride has the molecular shape
questions.explanation: Be has two bond pairs and no lone pair, so the molecule is linear (180°).

questions.stem: The molecular shape of boron trifluoride is
questions.explanation: Three bond pairs and no lone pair on boron give a trigonal planar molecule.

questions.stem: Methane has the molecular geometry
questions.explanation: Four bond pairs around carbon point toward the corners of a tetrahedron.

questions.stem: Gaseous phosphorus pentachloride is
questions.explanation: Five bond pairs around phosphorus adopt a trigonal bipyramid (three equatorial, two axial).

questions.stem: The molecular geometry of sulphur hexafluoride is
questions.explanation: Six S-F bond pairs and no lone pair give a regular octahedron.

questions.stem: Chlorine trifluoride has the molecular shape
questions.explanation: Three bond pairs and two lone pairs around chlorine give the T-shape (AX3E2).

questions.stem: The molecular shape of xenon difluoride is
questions.explanation: Two bond pairs and three lone pairs around Xe give a linear molecule (lone pairs equatorial in the TBP electron set).

questions.stem: Xenon tetrafluoride has the molecular shape
questions.explanation: Four bond pairs and two lone pairs (opposite each other) in an octahedral electron set give square planar XeF4.

questions.stem: Carbon dioxide is linear because the central carbon has
options: two bond domains and no lone pair
two lone pairs and no bonds
questions.explanation: Two regions of electron density (the two C=O bonds) lie 180° apart.

questions.stem: Sulphur dioxide is bent because sulphur has
options: one lone pair besides two bonding domains
three lone pairs and no bonds
questions.explanation: The SO2 electron geometry is trigonal planar; one corner is a lone pair, so the molecule is angular.

questions.stem: In PCl5 the axial P-Cl bonds, compared with the equatorial P-Cl bonds, are
questions.explanation: Each axial bond has three 90° neighbours, so it is longer and weaker than an equatorial bond.

questions.stem: Repulsion between electron pairs decreases in the order
options: bond pair-bond pair > lone pair-lone pair > lone pair-bond pair
lone pair-lone pair > lone pair-bond pair > bond pair-bond pair
lone pair-bond pair > lone pair-lone pair > bond pair-bond pair
questions.explanation: Lone pairs sit closer to the nucleus and occupy more space than bond pairs.

questions.stem: SF4 has a see-saw shape because sulphur is surrounded by
options: four bond pairs and one lone pair
five bond pairs and no lone pair
two lone pairs and three bond pairs
questions.explanation: Steric number 5 with one lone pair (equatorial) leaves a see-saw of four fluorines.

questions.stem: The molecular shape of BrF5 is
questions.explanation: Five bond pairs and one lone pair in an octahedral electron set give a square pyramid.

questions.stem: The molecular shape of the triiodide ion I3- is
questions.explanation: The central iodine has two bond pairs and three lone pairs; the ion is linear like XeF2.

questions.stem: The molecular shape of XeO3 is
questions.explanation: Xenon has three Xe=O bonds and one lone pair, so XeO3 is pyramidal (like NH3 in electron count of four domains).

questions.stem: The H-O-H angle is smaller than the H-N-H angle because
options: oxygen has two lone pairs while nitrogen has one
questions.explanation: Two lone pairs on oxygen compress the bond angle more than the single lone pair on nitrogen.

questions.stem: In a trigonal bipyramidal electron arrangement, a lone pair prefers
options: the nucleus of the central atom
a d orbital of a ligand atom
questions.explanation: Equatorial lone pairs have only two 90° neighbours instead of three, so they experience less repulsion.

questions.stem: The number of lone pairs on chlorine in ClF3 is
questions.explanation: Chlorine has seven valence electrons; three are used in Cl-F bonds, leaving two lone pairs (AX3E2).

questions.stem: The VSEPR notation AX3E2 corresponds to the molecular shape
questions.explanation: Three bonded atoms and two lone pairs give the T-shape, as in ClF3.

questions.stem: [PCl4]+ is tetrahedral whereas [PCl6]- is octahedral because
options: both ions have the same steric number
the steric numbers are 4 and 6 respectively
phosphorus is unhybridised in both ions
questions.explanation: Four bond pairs around P in [PCl4]+; six bond pairs around P in [PCl6]-.

questions.stem: The equatorial F-S-F angle in SF4 is less than 120° because
options: the axial bonds occupy more space than lone pairs
the equatorial lone pair compresses the adjacent F-S-F angle
fluorine atoms have no lone pairs
questions.explanation: lp-bp repulsion in the equatorial plane pushes the two equatorial fluorines together.

questions.stem: Hybridisation is the mixing of
options: atomic orbitals of similar energy on the same atom
molecular orbitals belonging to two different molecules
only d orbitals located on neighbouring atoms
questions.explanation: Atomic orbitals on one atom combine to give new hybrid orbitals used in bonding.

questions.stem: The hybridisation of carbon in methane is
questions.explanation: Four C-H sigma bonds require four equivalent sp3 hybrids.

questions.stem: Each carbon atom of ethene is
questions.explanation: Three sigma bonds (and one leftover p orbital for the pi bond) mean sp2 hybridisation.

questions.stem: Each carbon atom of ethyne is
questions.explanation: Two sigma bonds at 180° leave two p orbitals for the two pi bonds of the triple bond.

questions.stem: The hybridisation of boron in BF3 is
questions.explanation: Three B-F sigma bonds and no lone pair give steric number 3 and sp2 hybrids.

questions.stem: The hybridisation of beryllium in gaseous BeCl2 is
questions.explanation: Two Be-Cl bonds and no lone pair: steric number 2, sp hybridisation, linear molecule.

questions.stem: The hybridisation of phosphorus in PCl5 is
questions.explanation: Five P-Cl bonds require five hybrids: one 3s, three 3p and one 3d combine to give sp3d.

questions.stem: Steric number of a central atom equals
options: the number of sigma-bonded atoms plus the number of lone pairs
questions.explanation: Steric number is the count of electron domains and it fixes the hybridisation.

questions.stem: The hybridisation of nitrogen in ammonia is
questions.explanation: Three N-H bonds plus one lone pair give steric number 4, so nitrogen is sp3.

questions.stem: The hybridisation of oxygen in the water molecule is
questions.explanation: Two O-H bonds and two lone pairs: steric number 4, sp3 hybridisation.

questions.stem: The hybridisation of xenon in xenon difluoride is
questions.explanation: Two Xe-F bonds and three lone pairs give steric number 5 and sp3d hybrids.

questions.stem: The number of hybrid orbitals produced equals
options: the number of atomic orbitals that were mixed
twice the atomic number of the central atom
the number of pi bonds in the molecule
questions.explanation: n atomic orbitals mix to give n hybrids; none are created or destroyed.

questions.stem: Two sp hybrid orbitals on an atom are oriented at
questions.explanation: sp hybrids lie along a line, matching linear molecules such as BeCl2 and ethyne.

questions.stem: Three sp2 hybrid orbitals lie in a plane at angles of
questions.explanation: sp2 hybrids point toward the corners of an equilateral triangle.

questions.stem: See-saw SF4 uses which hybrid set on sulphur?
questions.explanation: Four S-F bonds and one lone pair: steric number 5, sp3d, see-saw shape.

questions.stem: Chlorine in ClF3 uses the hybridisation
questions.explanation: Three bonds and two lone pairs on chlorine give steric number 5 and sp3d hybrids.

questions.stem: The hybridisation of carbon in carbon dioxide is
questions.explanation: Carbon forms two sigma bonds and no lone pair (steric number 2), so it is sp hybridised.

questions.stem: The hybridisation of nitrogen in NH4+ is
questions.explanation: Four N-H sigma bonds and no lone pair: steric number 4, tetrahedral sp3 nitrogen.

questions.stem: A steric number of six on the central atom corresponds to
questions.explanation: Six electron domains require six hybrids: s + p + p + p + d + d = sp3d2.

questions.stem: Square planar XeF4 requires xenon hybridisation of
questions.explanation: Four bonds and two lone pairs give steric number 6, so xenon is sp3d2.

questions.stem: The hybridisation of sulphur in SO2 is
questions.explanation: Two S-O bonding domains and one lone pair: steric number 3, sp2 sulphur.

questions.stem: Carbon is sp3 in diamond but sp2 in graphite because
options: each carbon has four sigma neighbours in diamond and three planar sigma neighbours in graphite
both allotropes have the same hybridisation
diamond contains pi bonds between carbons
questions.explanation: Tetrahedral four-coordinate carbon is sp3; sheet-like three-coordinate carbon with a leftover p orbital is sp2.

questions.stem: The hybridisation of iodine in IF5 is
questions.explanation: Five I-F bonds and one lone pair give steric number 6 and sp3d2 (square pyramidal molecule).

questions.stem: In ethyne, each C-H bond is formed by overlap of
options: an sp hybrid on carbon with the 1s orbital of hydrogen
an sp2 hybrid on carbon with hydrogen 1s
an sp3 hybrid on carbon with hydrogen 1s
questions.explanation: Each carbon is sp; the two sp hybrids make the C-C sigma and the C-H sigma bonds.

questions.stem: Valence bond theory describes a covalent bond as
options: overlap of half-filled atomic orbitals on adjacent atoms
a sea of completely free electrons
a resonance hybrid of ions only
questions.explanation: VBT pictures a bond as shared electron density where two half-filled orbitals overlap.

questions.stem: Molecular orbital theory constructs MOs by
options: ignoring the atomic orbitals of the atoms
questions.explanation: Atomic orbitals of similar energy and symmetry mix to give bonding and antibonding molecular orbitals.

questions.stem: A well-known failure of simple VBT is that it cannot easily explain
options: the paramagnetism of the oxygen molecule
questions.explanation: A simple Lewis/VBT double bond in O2 has all electrons paired, but liquid oxygen is attracted into a magnet.

questions.stem: A bonding molecular orbital, compared with the parent atomic orbitals, is
questions.explanation: Constructive overlap lowers the energy; electrons in the bonding MO stabilise the molecule.

questions.stem: An antibonding MO is characterised by
options: electron density concentrated between the nuclei
a nodal plane between the nuclei
lower energy than the corresponding bonding MO
questions.explanation: Destructive interference puts a node between the atoms and raises the orbital energy.

questions.stem: MOT is especially useful, compared with simple VBT, when one needs
options: only a name for the hybridisation of methane
bond order and magnetic behaviour of diatomic species
questions.explanation: Filling MOs immediately gives (Nb − Na)/2 and the number of unpaired electrons.

questions.stem: According to the LCAO method, two atomic orbitals combine to give
options: two molecular orbitals, one bonding and one antibonding
questions.explanation: The number of MOs equals the number of AOs mixed: a bonding–antibonding pair from two AOs.

questions.stem: A limitation of simple VBT relative to MOT is that VBT
options: does not naturally give fractional bond orders or the unpaired electrons of O2-like molecules
forbids the existence of pi bonds
questions.explanation: MOT filling yields bond orders such as 2.5 and explains why O2 is paramagnetic; elementary VBT does not.

questions.stem: Bond order in molecular orbital theory is given by
questions.explanation: Half the difference between bonding and antibonding electrons is the MOT bond order.

questions.stem: Nitrogen molecule is assigned a MOT bond order of
questions.explanation: N2 has eight bonding and two antibonding valence electrons in the 2s/2p set, so bond order is (8 − 2)/2 = 3.

questions.stem: The fluorine molecule has a MOT bond order of
questions.explanation: F2 fills π* with four electrons; (8 − 6)/2 = 1, matching a single F-F bond.

questions.stem: Dioxygen is paramagnetic because MOT places
options: two unpaired electrons in the π* orbitals
no electrons in any antibonding orbital
questions.explanation: Hund filling of degenerate π*2p orbitals leaves two unpaired electrons, so O2 is attracted into a magnetic field.

questions.stem: Dinitrogen is diamagnetic because
options: all electrons are paired in its MO configuration
questions.explanation: The configuration of N2 has every MO either empty or doubly occupied.

questions.stem: For O2 and F2 the valence MO energy order has
questions.explanation: From O2 onwards the σ2pz orbital drops below the π2p pair.

questions.stem: B2 is paramagnetic according to MOT because
options: it has two unpaired electrons in the π2p set
all of its electrons are paired
questions.explanation: For B2 the π2p orbitals fill before σ2p; Hund’s rule puts one electron in each π orbital.

questions.stem: Dicarbon C2 has a MOT bond order of
questions.explanation: C2 has eight valence electrons in bonding MOs of the 2s/2p set after cancelling σ2s/σ*2s, giving bond order 2.

questions.stem: He2 is not a stable molecule because its MOT bond order is
questions.explanation: Both bonding and antibonding 1s MOs are filled: (2 − 2)/2 = 0, so there is no net bond.

questions.stem: The superoxide ion is paramagnetic because MOT gives it
options: one unpaired electron in a π* orbital
questions.explanation: O2- has one more electron than O2, so π* holds three electrons — one remains unpaired.

questions.stem: A higher MOT bond order generally means
options: that the species must be paramagnetic
questions.explanation: More net bonding electrons pull the nuclei closer and raise the dissociation enthalpy.

questions.stem: F2 is diamagnetic; its valence MO diagram contains
options: an odd total number of electrons
questions.explanation: Eighteen electrons (or 14 valence) fill every occupied MO in pairs, including the filled π* set.

questions.stem: The hydrogen molecule H2 has a MOT bond order of
questions.explanation: Two electrons occupy σ1s and none occupy σ*1s, so bond order is 1.

questions.stem: The number of unpaired electrons in O2 according to MOT is
questions.explanation: The two π*2p orbitals each hold one electron with parallel spins.

questions.stem: The number of valence electrons placed in the MOT of F2 is
questions.explanation: Each fluorine contributes seven valence electrons, so fourteen electrons fill the 2s/2p MO set.

questions.stem: N2 is more stable than O2 partly because
options: N2 has the higher bond order
questions.explanation: Bond order 3 (N2) versus 2 (O2) means a stronger, shorter bond in dinitrogen.

questions.stem: KO2 contains the superoxide ion, which MOT treats as
options: O2 with one extra electron in a π* orbital
questions.explanation: Potassium superoxide is K+ O2-; the extra electron enters π*, leaving the ion paramagnetic.

questions.stem: Bond order of O2+ is greater than that of O2 because ionisation
options: removes an electron from an antibonding π* orbital
removes an electron from a bonding orbital
questions.explanation: Taking an electron from π* raises bond order from 2 to 2.5, so O2+ is more tightly bound than O2.

questions.stem: N2+ has a lower bond order than N2 because the electron is lost from
questions.explanation: The HOMO of N2 is the bonding σ2p orbital; removing that electron drops bond order from 3 to 2.5.

questions.stem: Among O2, O2+ and O2-, the longest bond is expected for
questions.explanation: Bond orders are 2.5, 2 and 1.5 respectively, so superoxide has the weakest, longest link.

questions.stem: C2 is diamagnetic because its MOT configuration fills
options: the π2p set with four electrons and no unpaired electron
questions.explanation: For C2 the π2p orbitals are fully occupied (four electrons) and σ2p is empty, so all spins are paired.

questions.stem: Compared with F2, the cation F2+ has a
options: larger bond order, because an antibonding electron is removed
bond order that cannot be defined
questions.explanation: F2 bond order is 1; removing a π* electron gives F2+ bond order 1.5.

questions.stem: MOT predicts B2 to be paramagnetic while C2 is not because
options: B2 places two electrons in degenerate π2p orbitals, whereas C2 fills that set
C2 has unpaired electrons and B2 does not
questions.explanation: Two π2p electrons (B2) remain unpaired; four π2p electrons (C2) are paired.

questions.stem: The peroxide ion is assigned a MOT bond order of
questions.explanation: O2^2- has two more electrons than O2, both in π*; bond order falls from 2 to 1.

questions.stem: Which of N2, O2 and F2 has the largest MOT bond order?
questions.explanation: Bond orders are 3, 2 and 1 respectively, so dinitrogen is the most strongly bound.

questions.stem: Ionisation of O2 to O2+ is expected to
options: increase the bond order and shorten the bond
questions.explanation: Loss of a π* electron raises bond order (2 → 2.5), so the cation has a shorter, stronger bond.

questions.stem: Nitric oxide has an odd electron and a MOT bond order of
questions.explanation: NO has 15 electrons; after filling, bond order is 2.5 and one electron remains unpaired.

questions.stem: For B2, C2 and N2 the valence MO order places
options: no π orbitals in the scheme
questions.explanation: Molecules with Z ≤ 7 for each atom have the inverted order: (π2p) then (σ2p).

questions.stem: Intermolecular hydrogen bonding is possible when hydrogen is bonded to
questions.explanation: A highly electronegative F, O or N polarises H and can accept a hydrogen bond through a lone pair.

questions.stem: Hydrogen fluoride has an unusually high boiling point for its molecular mass mainly because of
options: an ionic lattice of HF units
questions.explanation: HF molecules associate through F-H···F links, so extra energy is needed to boil the liquid.

questions.stem: Ice floats on liquid water because hydrogen bonding in ice
options: packs the molecules more densely than in the liquid
creates an open cage, so ice is less dense than water
questions.explanation: Each oxygen in ice is tetrahedrally hydrogen-bonded, leaving empty space in the lattice.

questions.stem: Water boils much higher than H2S mainly because
options: sulphur is more electronegative than oxygen
water has the lower molecular mass and nothing else differs
questions.explanation: O-H···O hydrogen bonds are strong in water; S-H bonds are too weakly polar for comparable H-bonding.

questions.stem: Intermolecular hydrogen bonds occur
questions.explanation: They link one molecule’s δ+ hydrogen to a lone pair on F, O or N of another molecule.

questions.stem: Ammonia can take part in hydrogen bonding because
options: nitrogen is electronegative, bears a lone pair, and is bonded to hydrogen
carbon is bonded to hydrogen in ammonia
ammonia is the ionic salt NH4Cl
questions.explanation: N-H bonds are polar and the nitrogen lone pair can accept a hydrogen bond.

questions.stem: Methane does not form hydrogen bonds because
options: C-H bonds are not polar enough and carbon has no lone pair to accept H-bonds
questions.explanation: Hydrogen bonding needs H attached to F, O or N and a lone pair on a similar atom.

questions.stem: o-Nitrophenol boils lower than p-nitrophenol mainly because the ortho isomer has
options: intramolecular hydrogen bonding, which reduces intermolecular association
questions.explanation: The ortho OH and NO2 groups H-bond within the molecule, so molecules attract each other less strongly.

questions.stem: Among NH3, H2O and HF, the highest boiling point belongs to
questions.explanation: Each water molecule can form up to four hydrogen bonds, giving the most extensive network and bp 100 °C.

questions.stem: Ethanol boils higher than dimethyl ether of the same formula mass because
options: ethanol molecules form intermolecular hydrogen bonds
the ether has stronger hydrogen bonds than ethanol
questions.explanation: The OH group of ethanol H-bonds to neighbouring molecules; ether oxygen has no H attached for donation.

questions.stem: In ice, each oxygen is hydrogen-bonded in a
options: tetrahedral arrangement to four hydrogens (two covalent, two H-bonds)
questions.explanation: The open hexagonal ice structure has every O tetrahedrally surrounded, which lowers the density.

questions.stem: The strongest individual hydrogen bond among HF, H2O and NH3 is found in
questions.explanation: Fluorine is the most electronegative, so the H-bond in hydrogen fluoride is the strongest of the three.

questions.stem: Glycerol is highly viscous chiefly because of
options: extensive intermolecular hydrogen bonding among three OH groups per molecule
the complete absence of hydroxyl groups
questions.explanation: Three hydroxyl groups per molecule create a dense H-bond network that resists flow.

questions.stem: The hydrogen difluoride ion HF2- exists because
options: fluorine is unable to form hydrogen bonds
a strong, nearly symmetric hydrogen bond holds F-H-F together
hydrogen is covalently divalent like oxygen
questions.explanation: The very strong F-H···F interaction in HF2- is a classic strong hydrogen bond.

questions.stem: In the electron-sea model of metals, valence electrons are
options: localised in covalent pairs between two atoms
delocalised over the whole cation lattice
questions.explanation: Metal atoms contribute valence electrons to a mobile sea that binds the cations together.

questions.stem: Metals conduct electricity because
options: delocalised electrons are free to move under an applied field
they are always molten at room temperature
questions.explanation: The electron sea provides mobile charge carriers, so current flows easily.

questions.stem: Malleability of metals is explained by
options: layers of cations sliding while the electron sea still holds the crystal
questions.explanation: Non-directional metallic bonding survives deformation, so metals can be hammered into sheets.

questions.stem: Metallic lustre arises because
options: electrons in the sea absorb and re-emit visible light
metals are always coated with paint
questions.explanation: Oscillating surface electrons interact with visible photons, giving the characteristic shine.

questions.stem: Metallic bonding is typical of elements that have
options: closed-shell noble-gas configuration at room temperature
low ionisation enthalpy and vacant orbitals, i.e. metals
questions.explanation: Easy loss of valence electrons into a delocalised sea is the hallmark of metallic elements.

questions.stem: Thermal conductivity of metals is high because
options: mobile electrons (and phonons) transport kinetic energy through the lattice
heat travels only by radiation inside a metal
cations are fixed and electrons are absent
questions.explanation: Energetic electrons drift and collide, carrying heat from the hot end to the cold end.

questions.stem: The strength of metallic bonding generally increases with
options: fewer valence electrons and a larger atomic radius
more valence electrons and a smaller atom
decreasing charge on the metal cation
replacement of the electron sea by hydrogen bonds
questions.explanation: A higher electron density in a smaller cation lattice binds the metal more tightly (e.g. Cr, Fe vs Na).

questions.stem: A metal conducts in the solid state, whereas a typical ionic crystal does not, because
options: ionic solids already have free electrons
metals have a delocalised electron sea, while ions in a crystal are locked in place
ionic solids are always molten at room temperature
questions.explanation: Current in metals is carried by the electron sea; solid ionic lattices have no mobile charges until they melt.

questions.stem: A sigma bond is formed by
questions.explanation: Head-on overlap concentrates electron density along the internuclear axis and gives a sigma bond.

questions.stem: A pi bond is formed by
questions.explanation: Sideways overlap of two p orbitals produces electron density above and below the axis — a pi bond.

questions.stem: A triple bond between two atoms consists of
options: one sigma bond and two pi bonds
two sigma bonds and one pi bond
questions.explanation: The first link is always sigma; the remaining two are pi bonds from leftover p orbitals.

questions.stem: A double bond consists of
options: one sigma bond and one pi bond
four electrons placed only in sigma orbitals
questions.explanation: One pair is shared end-on (σ) and one pair is shared sideways (π).

questions.stem: In ethyne (C2H2) the number of sigma bonds is
questions.explanation: Two C-H sigma bonds plus one C-C sigma bond give three sigma bonds (the triple bond also has two pi bonds).

questions.stem: A carbon dioxide molecule contains
options: two sigma bonds and two pi bonds
four sigma bonds and no pi bond
questions.explanation: O=C=O has a sigma and a pi in each C=O unit, totalling 2σ + 2π.

questions.stem: In the Kekule description, benzene (C6H6) contains how many pi bonds?
questions.explanation: Three alternating C=C double bonds contribute three pi bonds (six delocalised pi electrons).

questions.stem: Ethene has how many pi bonds?
questions.explanation: The C=C double bond contributes one pi bond; the five C-H/C-C single links are all sigma.

questions.stem: Counting the ring and the C-H links, benzene contains how many sigma bonds?
questions.explanation: Six C-C sigma bonds in the ring plus six C-H sigma bonds give twelve sigma bonds.

questions.stem: The dinitrogen molecule contains
options: one sigma bond and two pi bonds
two sigma bonds and one pi bond
questions.explanation: N≡N is a triple bond: one head-on overlap and two sideways overlaps.

questions.stem: Allene H2C=C=CH2 contains
options: four sigma bonds and two pi bonds
six sigma bonds and two pi bonds
two sigma bonds and four pi bonds
eight sigma bonds and no pi bond
questions.explanation: Four C-H sigma + two C-C sigma = six sigma; each of the two double bonds adds one pi bond.

questions.stem: In carbon dioxide, each C=O unit contributes
options: two sigma bonds and no pi bond
one sigma and one pi, so the molecule has two sigma and two pi bonds overall
a C≡O triple bond on each side
questions.explanation: Each double bond is 1σ + 1π; two of them give the familiar 2σ + 2π count for CO2.
